name: Carlos Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm second in charge at Westfield, a four-hundred-sow pig unit with about three hundred hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the feed. My day starts at half six with a shower-in, because of the disease rules, then I walk the farrowing rooms, check the piglets and the sows that are due. Afternoons it's weaning, moving pens, or out on the sprayer if it's that time of year. I'm usually home by six to my rented cottage, unless something's farrowing badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers when they go right, pigs weaned per sow, feed conversion, that kind of thing. I'm a bit of a nerd for it. What gets me down is the smell on my clothes and the price swings, one month we're making money on every pig and the next we're losing twenty a head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I've used a chatbot to help write up our health plan for the vet, and to check a feed calculation. My manager Gordon thinks it's witchcraft, so I don't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That's what my gut says too, half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool for paperwork and that's about it. In the farm office I'd tell Gordon he was right not to worry. I wouldn't post, I'm not much for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine with it. I'd keep using it for the boring bits and get home a bit earlier. The things that actually threaten my job are swine fever and pig prices, not chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it a bit more for the health plan and the spray records, maybe save an hour a week. I'd keep saving and keep paying into the rental flat my brother Kenji and I own together. And I'd probably go for the unit manager job when Gordon retires in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that saved hour a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, go to the gym, which I keep promising myself. Or get to my brother's for Sunday lunch on time for once. Small stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned swine fever. How does that compare as a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's much bigger. If it got into the area, we'd lose the whole herd in a week and the farm would be shut for months. A chatbot can't do that to you.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a handy tool for paperwork and not much more, and tell his manager he was right not to worry. He wouldn't post about it.
S0.think: He'd be privately fine with it, saving a little time. His real threats are swine fever and pig prices, not chatbots.
S0.do: Uses AI a bit more for the health plan and spray records, saving about an hour a week. Keeps saving, keeps paying into the rental flat he owns with his brother and aims for the unit manager job when his boss retires.
S0.quote: If it got into the area, we'd lose the whole herd in a week and the farm would be shut for months. A chatbot can't do that to you.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos sets AI against the risks he already lives with, and disease is far bigger. He is a quiet AI user who hides it from his manager. His plan in a quiet world is straightforward: save, own property with his brother, step up when his boss retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: OK. Yeah. In pigs, I can see that one happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is coming whether we like it or not, so better to learn it than fight it. I'd probably say at the pig producers' meeting that units should share what's working. And that the government should help with training, but not throw money at everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think pig units are made for this. Cameras already count piglets, sensors check the air and the feed. In five years Westfield might need two people where it now needs five, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of units nearby had the camera and sensor systems running, then ask for training, probably in the second year. I'd use the AI tools more at home to get comfortable. I'd keep saving and stop thinking about buying a new truck, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. Like a vet visit where you're pretty sure the herd's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be the three that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Rob and Kasia from the weaner house, and maybe the part-time lad. They're good workers, Kasia especially. I'd feel bad, but I'd also think it's just how things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where Rob and Kasia stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we got bigger, maybe. More sows, same people, the cameras doing the counting. That's the kind of thing I'd suggest to the owners, but it's their call and their money.

S1.say: He'd say it's coming either way, so it's better to learn it than fight it. He'd suggest at the pig producers' meeting that units share what works, and support some government help with training without throwing money around.
S1.think: He thinks pig units are made for this, with cameras and sensors already common, and expects the farm to need two people instead of five. He wants to be one of the two.
S1.do: Waits until nearby units have camera and sensor systems working, then asks for training in about year two. Uses AI more at home to get comfortable, keeps saving and holds off on a new truck.
S1.feel: Uneasy but in control, like a routine vet visit.
S1.quote: In five years Westfield might need two people where it now needs five, and I'd want to be one of them.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos is pragmatic to the point of being blunt about colleagues losing work. He shows real regret for Kasia but treats job losses as normal change, then floats growth as a way to keep them. Classic steady adopter: watch the neighbours, then train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's mad. That's next lambing, as the sheep people would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep calm and look after your people. The government would have to do something big, like support payments, and the companies making the robots should pay their share of tax. I'd say that even though I don't usually go in for big government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a pig unit is one of the easiest farms to automate fully. It's indoors, it's repeatable and it's all data already. I wouldn't be one of the two that stays, there'd be none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop any big spending and look hard at the flat with Kenji, maybe sell it while prices hold. I'd ask the owners straight out what their plan is and push for a decent pay-off. Then I'd look for work in something that still needs a person's judgement, maybe animal welfare inspection or vet support, if those last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm a planner, and two years doesn't let you plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives you just enough time to see the cliff. Not enough to build a bridge. I'd use it to get my money safe, that's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the flat. Wouldn't property hold its value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not. If loads of people lose their jobs at once, who pays the rent? I genuinely don't know. That's the problem with this one, every normal rule might be wrong.

S2.say: He'd tell people to keep calm and look after their staff, and argue the government must do something big like support payments, with robot makers paying their share of tax, even though he usually distrusts big government.
S2.think: He thinks indoor pig units are among the easiest farms to automate fully, being repeatable and already full of data. In this picture nobody stays, himself included.
S2.do: Stops big spending at once and considers selling the flat he owns with his brother while prices hold. Asks the owners for their plan and pushes for a decent pay-off, then looks for work that needs human judgement, such as welfare inspection or vet support.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because as a planner he feels two years leaves no room to plan.
S2.quote: It gives you just enough time to see the cliff. Not enough to build a bridge.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture shakes Carlos's faith in normal rules, including property as a safe asset. He moves further towards government action than his centre views would usually allow. His exit plan points to human-judgement roles but he is unsure they would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. OK. Still fast, but now I can actually think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the industry to plan properly, so let's do it. Training for stock people, clear rules on animal welfare with robots, and some support for the people it hits hardest. Sensible stuff, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get two or three good years running the new systems before they run themselves. That's useful, it's money and experience. But I'd want a second skill lined up by about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd take the training on the camera and sensor systems as soon as a neighbour proved them. By year two I'd start a part-time course in animal health, probably vet nursing or welfare inspection. I'd keep the flat with Kenji but put more aside in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like a big feed price rise you know is coming next quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why animal health, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because even with robots, someone has to be responsible when animals suffer. I think the law will want a person signing off. That's a guess, but it's a sensible one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your brother say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji works in IT, so he'd say he told me so. He's been on at me to learn coding for years. I'd tell him I'd rather learn pigs properly than code badly.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for the industry to plan properly: training for stock workers, clear welfare rules for robots and support for those hit hardest. Sensible, not dramatic.
S3.think: He expects two or three good years running the new systems before they run themselves, which is valuable money and experience. He wants a second skill ready by about 2030.
S3.do: Trains on camera and sensor systems in year one once a neighbour has proved them, starts a part-time animal health course in year two and builds up cash while keeping the flat.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like a feed price rise expected next quarter.
S3.quote: I'd tell him I'd rather learn pigs properly than code badly.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Carlos's planner style; he lays out a clear two-step path. He bets that the law will keep a human responsible for animal welfare, and says it's a guess. His brother's IT career is a running point of comparison.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Right. That's plenty of time if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so no excuses for being caught out. I'd tell the young lads coming into pigs to learn the tech and the animals both. That's about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd see this as a chance. I could be unit manager by 2029, learn all the systems and then move into something like welfare or advisory work with a good name behind me. Ten years is a whole career at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the unit manager job when Gordon retires, and push the owners to bring in the proven systems step by step. I'd keep saving and keep the flat. Around year four or five I'd start the animal health course, so I've got it done before things really shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of background worry, like knowing the boiler's old but still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is a whole career. Do you think you'd actually use it, or put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say I'd use it. Honestly, I'd probably drift for a couple of years and then get a fright when a neighbour lays people off. That's usually how I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Westfield look like in 2036, in your picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same sheds, maybe twice the sows, and one person watching screens and walking the rooms. I'd want that person to be someone who still likes pigs. Otherwise it's just a factory, and people would be right to worry.

S4.say: He'd say a decade leaves no excuse for being caught out, and tell newcomers to pig farming to learn both the technology and the animals.
S4.think: He sees ten years as a chance: become unit manager by 2029, master the systems, then move into welfare or advisory work with a good reputation behind him.
S4.do: Goes for the unit manager job when his boss retires and pushes for proven systems step by step. Keeps saving and the flat, and starts an animal health course around year four or five.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a background worry like an old boiler that still works.
S4.quote: I'd probably drift for a couple of years and then get a fright when a neighbour lays people off. That's usually how I move.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Carlos frames AGI as a career ladder, though he admits he'd drift until something scares him. Each AGI picture adds a different trigger: fear at two years, planning at five, opportunity at ten. He wants the last person in the shed to be someone who still likes pigs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build that bridge. What would help is clear information about which jobs are actually going and when, plus some kind of support while people retrain. Not forever, just long enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The animals, maybe. Everyone talks about jobs, but if it's robots running pig units, who makes sure the pigs are all right? I'd want that taken seriously.

headlineQuote: It gives you just enough time to see the cliff. Not enough to build a bridge.
portrait: Carlos Ito is a 27-year-old second-in-charge at an indoor pig unit with its own arable land, a numbers person who quietly uses AI for paperwork. He's pragmatic and in the middle politically, adopting new systems once neighbours have proved them. He believes pig units are among the easiest farms to automate and is frank that colleagues would go first. In the fast picture he sees a cliff with no time for a bridge; with five or ten years he plans a move into animal health or welfare work. He owns a rental flat with his brother and treats savings as his main shock absorber.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is only enough to see the cliff, not to build a way across.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information on which jobs are going and when, and time-limited support while people retrain.
